newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE -Soccer violence rising in post-communist Romania.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE -Soccer violence rising in post-communist Romania.

text.p: Violence among armed gangs of soccer supporters is on the rise in Romania and commentators blame it on a general moral deterioration in the Balkan country in the seven years since the fall of communism.
Nearly all major Romanian teams are followed by groups of unruly supporters bearing a wide variety of primitive weapons. Some sport exotic names.
"You cannot dissociate the violence at a soccer stadium from Romania's social violence," junior Sports Minister Emeric Ienei, a former Romanian national team coach, told Reuters.
"If soccer is considered important, Romania's entire social fabric is in danger because violence in the stadiums is getting worse and worse."

This month supporters of Dinamo Bucharest started fires at the stadium of their main rival, Steaua Bucharest. They destroyed 700 seats before police herded them into a parking lot and pinpointed the troublemakers.
FANS SMUGGLE INCENDIARY BOMBS INTO STADIUM
Initial enquiries show the crowds were highly organised. Hundreds of fans sneaked primitive incendiary bombs past guards at the stadium -- in soft drink cans hidden in big base drums.
"We filled the cans with furniture varnish, which is inflamable and produces dense smoke," a Dinamo supporter told a local television channel.
Leaflets pasted on buildings before the game urged Dinamo fans: "Whoever is with us is against Steaua. Let's blow up Steaua stadium!"
Soccer authorities took quick action, ordering Dinamo to pay $20,000 for repairs. The club also got a $1,500 fine and was told to play its next two home games behind closed doors.

The courts may go even further. Fifty-nine fans remain in custody and could face up to 10 years in jail if convicted of arson. About 1,000 others got off with fines of up to $17, in a country where average monthly wages are less than $80.
On Romania's increasingly crime-ridden streets, soccer gangs roam before and after matches, smashing shop windows and car windscreens and sometimes hijacking buses.
Some adopt names like "Red Brigades", "Dracula Commando" or "New Ultra Army".
They seem little driven by the politics which used to motivate some Romanians to use soccer as a cloak to shout slogans against communist authority.
But plenty of "class consciousness" remains.
OLD RIVALRIES, HATREDS REMAIN

Fans of Steaua, traditionally representing the army, denounce supporters from Dinamo, long linked with the Interior Ministry, as "red dogs", the same taunt they used against the pervasive Securitate police under dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
Rapid Bucharest, the "working class" team associated with railway employees and the Transport Ministry, despises both its rivals in the capital as defenders of the "ruling classes".

Outside Bucharest, Universitatea Craiova, has the most feared fans. The club was ordered to play four consecutive home matches at a neutral stadium after their supporters smashed cars and buses in the southwestern city.

In the most violent incident of recent years, Rapid fans hurled stones at a train carrying supporters back to Pitesti two years ago. One person was killed and three carriages destroyed. A 16 year-old Steaua supporter was killed the same year in a knife fight with Rapid fans.

Soccer officials say part of the explanation for the increased violence may lie with the general decline in the national game. Dozens of talented players have been lured abroad by clubs paying top salaries and average attendance at matches has plunged to 3,000 from 16,000 in 1989.

"Romanians were frustrated for so long by communist oppression and are now following their instincts when they enter a stadium," the Romanian Soccer Federation's General Secretary, Adalbert Kassai, told Reuters.
He said fans were abetted by coaches, trainers and even bad refereeing.

"Team officials have often incited supporters by showing complete disregard for officiating decisions," he said. "The Federation has tried to act by banning referees after bad calls, sometimes for up to 12 matches. But these did not produce the right results."
This has even had international repercussions. No Romanian referee has been asked by FIFA or UEFA to officiate European or World Cup finals since the 1990 World Cup in Italy.
